The general scientific consensus, as stated by multiple authoritative sources, is that somatic mutations are not passed to offspring [d3][d5][d6][d9][d12]. Somatic mutations occur in non-reproductive body cells and are passed only to daughter cells via mitosis, not to offspring via sexual reproduction, because traits are transmitted through germline (sperm and egg) cells [d6][d5]. However, this rule has important exceptions: research on Elkhorn coral (Acropora palmata) demonstrated that approximately 50% of somatic mutations in a parent coral were inherited by uniparental offspring, suggesting that in some organisms the separation between somatic and germline cells is incomplete [d1][d2][d7][d8]. Similarly, in hermaphroditic plants, somatic mutations accumulated during vegetative growth can be inherited by offspring through self-fertilization [d10][d11]. Wikipedia's entry on somatic mutations explicitly acknowledges both the general rule and its exceptions, noting that "many organisms simply do not dedicate a separate germline during early development" [d4]. Thus, whether somatic mutations are passed to offspring depends on the organism: in most animals the answer is no, but in corals, plants, and other organisms with late or incomplete germline segregation, somatic mutations can be inherited [d1][d4][d8].
